[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Python Magic Methods"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Magic methods in Python are special methods that begin and end with double underscores (e.g., __init__, __str__). They are also known as 'dunder' methods (short for 'double underscore'). These methods provide a way to implement operator overloading, customize class behavior, and integrate seamlessly with Python's built-in functions."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"The __init__ Method: Constructor"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The __init__ method is the constructor for a class. It's called when an object is created from the class. It's used to initialize the object's attributes."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def greet(self):
        print(f"Hello, my name is {self.name} and I am {self.age} years old.")

person1 = Person("Alice", 30)
person1.greet()"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the example above, __init__ takes 'name' and 'age' as arguments and assigns them to the object's attributes 'self.name' and 'self.age'."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"The __str__ Method: String Representation"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The __str__ method defines the "informal" string representation of an object. It's called by the 'str()' function and the 'print()' function. It should return a human-readable string."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, author):
        self.title = title
        self.author = author

    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.title} by {self.author}"

book = Book("The Lord of the Rings", "J.R.R. Tolkien")
print(book)  # Output: The Lord of the Rings by J.R.R. Tolkien
str(book) # Output: 'The Lord of the Rings by J.R.R. Tolkien'"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Here, __str__ returns a string that describes the book's title and author. When 'print(book)' is called, Python uses the __str__ method to get the string representation of the 'book' object."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"The __repr__ Method: Unambiguous Representation"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The __repr__ method defines the "official" string representation of an object. It's called by the 'repr()' function. It should return a string that can be used to recreate the object. If possible, this should be a valid Python expression."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point(x={self.x}, y={self.y})"

point = Point(2, 3)
print(repr(point))  # Output: Point(x=2, y=3)
point # Output: Point(x=2, y=3)"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, __repr__ returns a string that looks like the code needed to create the 'Point' object. When you type 'point' in the interactive interpreter, it calls the __repr__ method."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If __str__ is not defined, Python will use __repr__ as a fallback for 'str()'."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"It's generally recommended to always define __repr__ for your classes, as it provides a useful debugging tool."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Other Useful Magic Methods"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"__len__(self): Defines the behavior for when 'len()' is called on an object."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"__getitem__(self, key): Defines the behavior for when an item is accessed using square brackets (e.g., obj[key])."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"__setitem__(self, key, value): Defines the behavior for when an item is assigned using square brackets (e.g., obj[key] = value)."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"__delitem__(self, key): Defines the behavior for when an item is deleted using 'del obj[key]'."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"__iter__(self): Returns an iterator for the object."},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"__next__(self): Returns the next item from the iterator."},{"order":24,"type":"bullet_point","text":"__add__(self, other): Defines the behavior for the addition operator (+)."},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"By implementing these and other magic methods, you can create classes that behave like built-in Python types and provide a more intuitive and Pythonic interface."}]
